simonmarais-2022-a1.prompt:
Let $ABCD$ be a unit square, and let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the points on $AB$ and $AD$, respectively, such that $AEPF$ is a rectangle. Let $x$ and $y$ denote the lengths of $AE$ and $AF$, respectively.

Determine a two-variable polynomial $f(x, y)$ with the property that the area of $AEPF$ is greater than the area of each of the quadrilaterals $EBCP$ and $FPCD$ if and only if $f(x, y) > 0$.

simonmarais-2022-a2.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $S$ be a set with $2^n$ elements. Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ be randomly and independently chosen subsets of $S$, where each possible subset of $S$ is chosen with equal probability. Let $P_n$ be the probability that
$$A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n = S \qquad\text{and}\qquad A_1 \cap A_2 \cap \cdots \cap A_n = \emptyset.$$

Prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} P_n = \frac{1}{e^2}$.
simonmarais-2022-a2.answer: Elementwise independence gives $P_n=(1-2^{1-n})^{2^n}$, and $(1-\frac2N)^N\to e^{-2}$ as $N=2^n\to\infty$.

simonmarais-2022-a3.prompt:
Let $0 < a < 1$ be a fixed real number. Show that there are at least two values of $x$ in the interval $(0, 1)$ such that
$$\int_0^x \left( \sin\!\left( \frac{\pi \sin \frac{\pi t}{2}}{2} \right) + \frac{2}{\pi} \arcsin\!\left( \frac{2}{\pi} \arcsin t \right) - 2t \right) \mathrm{d}t = \frac{1}{2} \left( a - \frac{2}{\pi} \arcsin\!\left( \frac{2}{\pi} \arcsin a \right) \right) \left( \sin\!\left( \frac{\pi \sin \frac{\pi a}{2}}{2} \right) - a \right).$$
simonmarais-2022-a3.answer: With $f(t)=\sin(\frac\pi2\sin\frac{\pi t}2)$ and $g=f^{-1}$, the left side is $F(x)=\int_0^x(f+g-2t)$, which satisfies $F(0)=F(1)=0$ and $F(a)=\int_{g(a)}^a(f-a)$, larger than the right side (a triangle under the concave graph of $f$); apply the intermediate value theorem on $(0,a)$ and $(a,1)$.

simonmarais-2022-a4.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $q \ge 3$ be an odd integer such that every prime factor of $q$ is larger than $n$. Prove that
$$\frac{1}{n!\,(q-1)^n} \prod_{i=1}^{n} (q^i - 1)$$
is an integer that has no prime factor in common with $\dfrac{q-1}{2}$.
simonmarais-2022-a4.answer: Write the number as $X=\prod_{i\le n}\frac{[i]_q}{i}$ with $[i]_q=\frac{q^i-1}{q-1}$; for $p\le n$ the multiplicative order of $q$ modulo $p^{a+v_p(q-1)}$ is at most $p^a$, giving integrality; and for $p\mid\frac{q-1}2$ the binomial expansion of $(1+2m)^i-1$ shows $v_p([i]_q)=v_p(i)$.

simonmarais-2022-b1.prompt: Let $A > 1$ be a real number. Determine all pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers for which there exists a positive real number $x$ such that $(1 + x)^m = (1 + Ax)^n$.

simonmarais-2022-b2.prompt:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be real numbers, and let $P$ be the polynomial
$$P(x) = x^6 + ax^4 + bx^2 + c.$$
Suppose that there is a unique circle $\Gamma$ in the complex plane such that all of the roots of $P$ lie on $\Gamma$. Prove that $b^3 = a^3 c$.
simonmarais-2022-b2.answer: The root set is symmetric under $w\mapsto-w$, so uniqueness forces $\Gamma$ to be centred at $0$; then the roots $z_i$ of $z^3+az^2+bz+c$ all have modulus $\rho$, so $\bar z_i=\rho^2/z_i$ gives $b=ac/\rho^2$ and $c^2=\rho^6$, whence $b^3=a^3c$.

simonmarais-2022-b3.prompt:
Ari and Sam are playing a game in which they take turns breaking a block of chocolate in two and eating one of the pieces. At each stage of the game the block of chocolate is a rectangle with integer side lengths. On each player's turn, they break the block of chocolate into two such rectangles along a horizontal or vertical line, and eat the piece with smaller area. (If the two pieces have the same area they may eat either one.) The game ends when the block of chocolate is a $1 \times 1$ rectangle, and the winner is the last player to take their turn breaking the chocolate in two.

At the start of the game the block of chocolate is a $58 \times 2022$ rectangle. If Ari goes first, which player has a winning strategy?

simonmarais-2022-b4.prompt:
*The following problem is open in the sense that the answer to part (b) is not currently known. A solution to part (a) will be awarded 7 points. Up to 7 additional points may be awarded for progress on part (b).*

Let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ and $b_0, b_1, b_2, \ldots$ be two sequences of positive integers, satisfying $a_0 b_0 \ge 600$ and
$$\begin{aligned} a_{n+1} &= a_n + 2 \cdot \lfloor b_n / 20 \rfloor, \\ b_{n+1} &= b_n + 3 \cdot \lfloor a_n / 30 \rfloor, \end{aligned}$$
for all $n \ge 0$.

(a) Prove that there exists a nonnegative integer $N$ such that
$$-13 \le a_n - b_n \le 23,$$
for all $n \ge N$.

(b) Must there exist a nonnegative integer $n$ such that $a_n = b_n$?

*Here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$.*
simonmarais-2022-b4.answer: (a) $d_n=a_n-b_n$ satisfies $\frac9{10}d_n-2<d_{n+1}<\frac9{10}d_n+3$, so it is eventually in $[-19,29]$ and monotone outside $[-10,20]$; if it stayed in $[24,29]$ or $[-19,-14]$ it would be eventually constant, and then a mod-$6$ argument forces $q_{n+1}=\frac{11}{10}q_n$ for integers $q_n$, impossible. (b) is an **open problem**.
simonmarais-2022-b4.reviewNote: Part (b) is an open problem (stated as such on the paper); only part (a) is proved. Consider excluding from practice or treating as part (a) only.

simonmarais-2022-c3.prompt:
A grasshopper is sitting on the number line. Initially, it is sitting at the number $0$. Each second it jumps one unit to the left or to the right, with equal probability. The directions of the jumps are chosen independently of each other.

Let $p$ denote the probability that, after $2022$ jumps, the grasshopper is sitting at a number divisible by $5$. Determine whether $p < \frac{1}{5}$, $p = \frac{1}{5}$, or $p > \frac{1}{5}$.

simonmarais-2022-c4.prompt:
A machine is programmed to output a sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$. It outputs the integers independently, one at a time, and at each step the probability that it outputs the integer $k$ is equal to $\dfrac{1}{2^k}$. The machine stops when it outputs an integer that it has already output before.

Prove that the probability that the machine stops when it has output exactly $n$ integers is
$$\frac{(n-1)!\,(2^n - n - 1)}{\displaystyle\prod_{r=1}^{n} (2^r - 1)}.$$
simonmarais-2022-c4.answer: $P(\text{first }n\text{ outputs distinct})=n!\,T(n)$ with $T(n)=\sum_{0<a_1<\dots<a_n}2^{-(a_1+\dots+a_n)}$; splitting on $a_1=1$ gives $T(n)=\frac{T(n-1)}{2^n-1}$, so this probability is $\prod_{r\le n}\frac r{2^r-1}$, and the answer is the difference of consecutive values.
